title: How to Validate Customer Artwork on Teelaunch Before It Prints
excerpt: Custom print-on-demand orders fail at the upload step, not in production. This walkthrough covers the file, color, placement and rights checks that keep Teelaunch artwork from turning into reprints and refunds.
body: Custom artwork is the highest margin line in a print-on-demand catalog and the easiest one to lose money on. A buyer uploads a low resolution photo, the print comes back soft, and you pay for a replacement, a return label and a review that mentions quality. The failure rarely happens in production. It happens at upload, where nobody checked whether the file survives being printed twelve inches wide. Your print partner prints what you send, so the validation layer has to be yours.

Start with file rules, and put them where the buyer sees them before upload rather than on a policy page nobody opens. Ask for three hundred DPI at true print size, which for a twelve inch chest print means roughly thirty six hundred pixels on the long edge. Accept PNG with a transparent background for artwork on the garment, and SVG or PDF for logos. Enforce the rules at the form, not by email afterwards, because a buyer asked to resend a file usually asks for a refund instead.

Color is the second pass. Screens are backlit and ink on fabric is not, so neon, deep gradients and photographs with heavy shadow all lose something in the transfer. Tell buyers which colors shift, and offer a flat color version for the risky art. Keep a reference print of each fabric so you describe what to expect in plain words. If a design depends on exact brand colors, run a paid sample before you sell it. Guessing on color costs more in replacements than the sample ever costs.

Placement is the third pass, and it is where most amateur mockups go wrong. Every product needs a template with true print dimensions and a safe area that excludes seams, zippers, pockets and collars. Give each template a bleed margin and a centering tolerance, and reject anything that puts text across a seam. Keep the templates in one folder named by SKU so whoever checks artwork on a Monday morning sees the same file you used to build the listing. Approve placement before color, because fixing a wrong size later means a full reprint.

Rights and moderation belong on the same checklist. Buyer uploaded logos, sports crests and celebrity photos can put you on the wrong side of a trademark complaint even when the order is legitimate. Add a rights confirmation at checkout, publish a short list of what you will not print, and state the turnaround rule: the clock starts when artwork is approved, not when the order is placed. That sentence protects you when a buyer sits on a proof for four days and then asks where the parcel is. Keep three rejection messages ready so declining an order takes one click.

Then run the queue rather than the exceptions. Hold every order with unapproved artwork in one view, remind at twenty four and seventy two hours, and decide in advance what happens at day five: refund, substitute a stock design, or cancel. Log the reason for each rejection so a pattern shows up in the monthly review, and tighten the upload rules when the same problem appears three times. The DTCwise Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and /tool/teelaunch covers the production detail behind artwork handling.
